The core duality lies between hardware-dependent optical tracking and broadcast-derived interpolation. The former offers full spatiotemporal resolution but is economically inaccessible; the latter democratizes access but introduces gaps due to camera visibility constraints. The external load estimator operates under the assumption that work done by an athlete is measurable through kinematic variables—distance and acceleration—which are derived from interpolated coordinates. These estimates fail when data is missing or corrupted, particularly during off-screen periods. The broadcast tracking interpolator bridges this gap by reconstructing trajectories using computer vision, yet its accuracy hinges on consistent camera coverage and temporal sampling rates. Subtrack segmentation addresses discontinuities by splitting long tracks into manageable segments, enabling localized load calculations. Each primitive must account for sparsity and noise inherent in broadcast data, ensuring robustness in downstream analytics.
